newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian strikers meet government over pay woes.
newsitem.headline: Albanian strikers meet government over pay woes.

text.p: Tens of thousands of Albanian public sector workers staged a one-hour warning strike on Monday, demanding full compensation from the government for recent price hikes in basic goods and rising inflation.
"The warning strike aims at drawing the attention of the people and the government to our problems," Estref Mersinaj of the Independent Trade Union (ITU) told Reuters.

Another ITU official said the government had agreed to meet a union delegation to hear their demands. "We shall see what the government decides and a one-day strike may be held in two weeks," he said.
A government official confirmed the meeting was under way on Monday afternoon, but declined to give details.
Mersinaj said workers wanted compensation for increased bread, gas and kerosene prices after those were liberalised by the conservative government of President Sali Berisha in July.
They also want to be reimbursed for inflation gains after the introduction of a new tariff system and value-added tax.
Bread prices have been a sensitive issue since Albania toppled its hardline communist regime in 1990. More than 40 people were killed in a wave of food riots in 1991.

Workers in the areas of education, energy, health care, telecommunications, transport and in Albania's light industry participated in Monday's protests, organised by the ITU jointly with the Confederation of Albanian Trade Unions.
Union officials said the participation was almost 100 percent across the small Balkan nation.

The strike coincided with the first day of school at the country's secondary schools, affecting more than 700,000 pupils, officials said. There were no reports of power outages or unusual disruptions in the public transport network.

The government supplements the income of all public sector employees and pensioners with subsidies of 150-250 leks (about $17-28) per month to compensate for increased bread prices, but trade unions say that was not enough. "We want 100 percent compensation," Mersinaj said.

Imported wheat and flour are still excluded from both customs tariffs and value-added tax while bakeries continue to receive subsidies for electricity, water and fuel, but the introduction VAT and a new customs law has significantly increased most other prices in the small Balkan nation.
Albania's consumer prices rose 16.1 percent in August from the same month a year ago and were up 1.9 percent from July.
The government still controls prices of electricity, petrol and water.
